segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I watched when the Lamb opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures saying, as with a voice of thunder,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I looked, and there was a white horse, and the one seated on it had a bow; and a wreath was given to him, and he went out conquering, and in order to conquer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And another horse came out, fiery red, and it was given to the one seated on it to take peace from the earth, so that people would slaughter one another; and a great sword was given to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I looked, and there was a black horse, and the one seated on it had a pair of scales in his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I heard what sounded like a voice in the midst of the four living creatures, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “A quart of wheat for a denarius, and three quarts of barley for a denarius; and do not damage the oil and the wine!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I looked, and there was a pale green horse, and the one seated on it was named Death, and Hades was following with him. And authority was given to them over a fourth of the earth, to kill with the sword and with famine and with plague, and by the wild beasts of the earth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slaughtered because of the word of God and because of the testimony they held.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they cried out with a loud voice, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How long, Master, holy and true, before you pass judgment and avenge our blood on those who live on the earth?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And a white robe was given to each of them, and they were told to rest a little while longer, until the number was complete of their fellow slaves and their brothers and sisters who were about to be killed as they themselves had been.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I watched when he opened the sixth seal, and there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth made of hair, and the whole moon became like blood,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the stars of the sky fell to the earth, as a fig tree drops its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the sky was split apart like a scroll rolling up, and every mountain and island was moved from its place.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the kings of the earth and the nobles and the commanders and the rich and the powerful, and every slave and free person, hid themselves in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they said to the mountains and the rocks,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Fall on us and hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for the great day of their wrath has come, and who is able to stand?”

notes.note: The command is a single word and most naturally summons each horseman, who then appears. Some manuscripts add “and see”, making it an invitation to John; the King James Version follows that reading. The same applies in verses 3, 5 and 7.

The word normally means the wreath awarded to a victor or worn at a festival, not a king's crown, for which Revelation uses a different word (diadem). Most translations say “crown”. Here the wreath fits a rider who goes out to conquer. Who this rider is remains disputed: some take him as Christ, others as military conquest, the first of four calamities.

notes.phrase: A quart of wheat for a denarius
notes.traditional: A measure of wheat for a penny
notes.note: The measure (a choinix, a little over a litre) was roughly one person's daily ration of grain, and a denarius was a typical day's wage for a labourer. These are famine prices, many times the normal rate: a day's work buys only enough wheat for the worker alone, or enough of the cheaper barley for a small family. The command to spare the oil and the wine is variously explained, and its exact point is uncertain.

The word is the ordinary Greek term for the green of plants, and Revelation uses it of grass elsewhere. Applied to people it describes the sickly, greenish pallor of illness or fear, which suits a horse ridden by Death. Most translations say “pale”; some say “pale green” or “ashen”.

The Greek word is the same as the rider's name, Death, and could be rendered “death” here too. In the Septuagint, however, it regularly translates the Hebrew word for pestilence, and the list here echoes the four judgments of Ezekiel 14:21: sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence. Most modern translations therefore have “plague” or “pestilence”.

This is not the usual word for “Lord” but the term for the master of a household and owner of slaves, also used of rulers with absolute authority. Many translations render it “Sovereign Lord” or simply “Lord”. “Master” keeps it distinct from the usual word and fits the next verse, where the martyrs' companions are called their fellow slaves.

The word denotes those who are slaves of the same master, and it answers the address “Master” in the previous verse. Most translations soften it to “fellow servants”. The term was not demeaning in this setting: in the Septuagint, “slave of the Lord” is an honoured title for Moses and the prophets.

notes.traditional: until the number should be complete
notes.note: The Greek says only “until they were made complete”; “the number” is supplied, as in most translations, on the understanding that a set number of martyrs must be reached. It could also mean until they had completed their course, and some manuscripts have an active form that favours this.

The same Greek word means both the visible sky and God's dwelling. Here and in verse 14 the visible sky is in view, with its stars falling and its expanse rolling up, so “sky” is used, as in most modern translations. Older versions have “heaven”.

notes.phrase: Fall on us and hide us
notes.note: The cry echoes Hosea 10:8, and the whole scene of verses 12 to 17 draws on the prophets' pictures of the day of the Lord: the darkened sun and blood-red moon (Joel 2), the sky rolled up like a scroll and stars falling like figs (Isaiah 34:4), and people hiding among the rocks from God's presence (Isaiah 2). The closing question, “who is able to stand?”, likewise recalls Joel 2:11 and Malachi 3:2.

Many manuscripts read “his wrath”, which the King James Version follows. The reading “their”, referring to both the one on the throne and the Lamb, has strong early support and is adopted by most modern editions; “his” is probably a scribal adjustment to the mention of the Lamb's wrath in the previous verse.

candidates.reason: Recurs across Paul, James, 1 Peter and Revelation, where “crown” blurs the distinction from διάδημα and translators split between “crown” and “wreath”.
Used of God, Christ and slave-owners in several books and rendered variously as “Lord”, “Sovereign Lord” and “Master”; it should be kept distinct from κύριος.
Should follow whatever is decided for δοῦλος (slave or servant) so that the two do not diverge between chapters.
Frequent of divine judgment across the New Testament; translators vary between “wrath” and “anger”, and readers would notice inconsistency.
Ranges over “soul”, “life”, “self” and “person” throughout the New Testament and needs sense-by-sense guidance to keep chapters consistent.
